transcript.text: Price Signals
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-01
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain how prices coordinate buyers, sellers, and resource allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Prices coordinate decentralized decisions by communicating scarcity and changing the incentives facing buyers and sellers. Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal. A higher price raises the cost of consuming the good and encourages substitution or conservation. A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses. A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses.
The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads.
A congested road has no toll.
A price rises while quantity sold also rises.
A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to assume that a higher price always tells buyers and sellers to do the same thing. It discourages quantity demanded while encouraging quantity supplied, coordinating opposite responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: USING A PRICE SIGNAL

A hospital posts current wait times of 90 minutes at Clinic A and 20 minutes at Clinic B. Patients who can use either location shift toward Clinic B. The posted wait acts like a nonmoney price signal: it communicates relative congestion and reallocates demand without changing the medical fee.
CHECK YOURSELF
What response does a higher market price normally encourage from sellers?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Tax Wedges and Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
WATCH OUT
Do not use pre tax quantity or buyer price change only. The tax is $46 - $34 = $12. Tax revenue is $12 × 420 = $5,040.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TAX REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price in dollars. Demand slopes down. Supply slopes up, intersecting demand at quantity 100 and price 15. A parallel Supply + tax curve above supply intersects demand at quantity 80 and price 18. At quantity 80, original supply is at price 12. Dashed guides also mark prices 10 and 20 and quantities 65, 120 and 150.

The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?

Market Failures
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-03
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Identify externalities, public goods, market power, and corrective policy logic.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A market failure occurs when private decisions do not produce an efficient allocation of resources. An externality affects people outside the transaction. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude.
Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.
A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse government provision with the economic definition of a public good. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING AN EXTERNALITY

A factory's production imposes $8 of pollution damage per unit on nearby residents, but the factory pays only its $20 private marginal cost. Social marginal cost is $20 + $8 = $28. If buyers' marginal benefit is $24, the unit looks worthwhile privately but destroys $4 of social surplus, demonstrating an external-cost market failure.
CHECK YOURSELF
What makes an effect an externality?

Price Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-04
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand and interpret the result
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change: PED = absolute percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. The midpoint method uses the average of the two quantities and the average of the two prices, so reversing the direction gives the same result. Demand is elastic when PED is greater than 1, unit elastic at 1, and inelastic below 1. Elasticity uses percentages, not raw unit changes or visual slope. Close substitutes, a longer adjustment period, a larger budget share, and a narrower market definition generally make demand more elastic.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Two price-quantity points are provided for a midpoint calculation.
The problem asks whether the quantity response is elastic, unit elastic, or inelastic.
Substitutes, time to adjust, budget share, or market scope are changing.
A linear demand curve has constant slope but different elasticity along the line.
A horizontal or vertical demand curve represents a limiting elasticity case.
WATCH OUT

A steeper-looking curve is not automatically less elastic. Slope uses the original price and quantity units, while elasticity compares percentage changes and depends on the price-quantity location. Put percentage quantity change in the numerator, use midpoint averages in both denominators, and classify demand using the absolute value of PED.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MIDPOINT ELASTICITY

Price elasticity of demand. Vertical axis: Price, from 0 to 20. Horizontal axis: Quantity, from 0 to 150. The straight downward Demand curve runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Labeled points are C at quantity 30 and price 12, B at quantity 60 and price 8, and A at quantity 90 and price 4. Dashed guides connect each point to its axis values. C to B supplies the worked example; B to A supplies the self-check.

Between C and B, price falls from $12 to $8 while quantity demanded rises from 30 to 60. Using midpoint values, quantity changes by 66.7% and price changes by 40.0%, so PED = 66.7% / 40.0% = 1.67. Because 1.67 is greater than 1, demand is elastic over this interval: quantity responds proportionally more than price changes.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using points B (P = $8, Q = 60) and A (P = $4, Q = 90), what is midpoint PED, and how should demand be classified over that interval?

Price Elasticity of Supply
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-05
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Measure Price Elasticity of Supply.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price elasticity of supply measures the percentage response of quantity supplied to a one-percent change in price. Price Elasticity of Supply measures and interprets how quantity supplied responds to price changes, including time horizon, capacity, storage, determinants, and midpoint calculations. Storage creates another margin through which sellers can respond to price changes. Investment and capacity adjustment make long-run supply more responsive. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a percentage change in quantity supplied caused by a percentage change in the good's price.
Compute elasticity as percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
A larger elasticity means sellers respond more strongly to the price change.
Supply is usually more elastic when firms have more time or spare capacity to adjust production.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse supply elasticity with demand shifters. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN VERSUS LONG-RUN SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Upward-sloping SR supply is steeper than upward-sloping LR supply. Both pass through quantity 60 and price 4. At price 8, point A on SR supply is at quantity 70 and point B on LR supply is at quantity 100. Dashed guides connect those values to the axes.

The price rises from $4 to $8. On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10/65 = 15.4%; the midpoint price change is 4/6 = 66.7%. Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4%/66.7% = 0.23, which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?

Income Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-06
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Income Elasticity of Demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Income elasticity of demand measures how demand changes when consumer income changes. Income elasticity helps firms anticipate demand shifts as consumer income changes. Different income responses shift the composition of demand as purchasing power changes. Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income. A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises.
A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls.
A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6.
Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misread the sign of income elasticity. A positive coefficient identifies a normal good; a negative coefficient identifies an inferior good.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING INCOME ELASTICITY

Household income rises by 10%, and demand for restaurant meals rises by 15%. Income elasticity is 15% / 10% = 1.5. The positive sign identifies restaurant meals as a normal good, and the coefficient above 1 indicates that demand responds more than proportionally to income in this example.
CHECK YOURSELF
Income changes by 5 percent and demand for premium gym memberships changes by 8 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?

Elasticity and Total Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.

Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-10
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Consumer surplus is the difference between a buyer's willingness to pay and the price actually paid. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Demand can be interpreted as buyers' marginal willingness to pay. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a buyer's willingness to pay and the market price actually paid.
Individual consumer surplus equals willingness to pay minus price.
On a graph, consumer surplus is the area below demand and above the market price up to the quantity traded.
A buyer whose willingness to pay is below price does not purchase and earns no consumer surplus.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume every trade creates surplus. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING CONSUMER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.

At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The demand intercept of $30 represents the highest willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is the triangle above price and below demand: 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64.
CHECK YOURSELF

THE CORE IDEA

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.

The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.

Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.

Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.

A common mistake is to equate more output with more efficiency. The forced extra unit contributes $23 - $29 = -$6 to total surplus.

Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects

MICRO-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price or policy change can transfer surplus between buyers and sellers and can destroy surplus by preventing mutually beneficial trades. A transfer changes who receives existing gains without changing their total. Deadweight loss is different: it represents gains from exchange that disappear because quantity moves away from the efficient level.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to count only existing buyers or only new buyers. With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.

Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-15
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Efficiency concerns the size of total surplus, while equity concerns how benefits and costs are distributed. The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use total surplus to evaluate efficiency and distributional evidence to evaluate equity.
Recognize that the allocation with the largest total surplus need not be the most equal.
Remember that measured willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay.
A policy judgment requires an explicit value choice when efficiency and equity point in different directions.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat efficiency as equity. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING EFFICIENCY AND EQUITY

Policy A creates $500 of total surplus divided evenly between buyers and sellers. Policy B creates $520 of total surplus but gives $500 to sellers and $20 to buyers. Policy B is more efficient because total surplus is larger, but whether its distribution is more equitable is a separate normative judgment.

Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.

THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

MICRO-17
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

International trade changes consumer and producer surplus and creates net gains when the world price differs from the no-trade equilibrium price. The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.
Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume trade has only winners or only losers. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers. The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.

MICRO-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Economic cost includes both explicit payments and the implicit opportunity costs of owner-supplied resources. Explicit costs require cash payments to outside suppliers, while implicit costs measure the value of income or returns forgone by using the owner's time, money, or property in the business. Economic decisions count both because every resource has a next-best use.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Classify cash payments to outside suppliers as explicit costs.
Identify the income or return sacrificed on owner-supplied time, money, or property as an implicit cost.
Economic cost includes both explicit and implicit opportunity costs.
Do not treat an owner-supplied resource as free merely because no check is written.

A common mistake is to count only recorded expense. Economic cost equals explicit cost plus all implicit opportunity costs: $70,000 + $40,000 + $5,000.

A business pays $70,000 in wages and rent. The owner also gives up a $40,000 salary and $5,000 of interest that invested capital could have earned elsewhere. Explicit cost is $70,000; implicit cost is $45,000; economic cost is $70,000 + $45,000 = $115,000.

Accounting, Economic & Normal Profit

MICRO-19
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate and interpret accounting profit, economic profit, implicit costs, and normal profit.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs from revenue, while economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs. Normal profit is the return required to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use, so it is included among implicit costs. Zero economic profit therefore means the firm covers every explicit and implicit cost, not that the owner receives nothing.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Start with total revenue and identify both explicit and implicit costs.
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs only; economic profit subtracts both kinds of cost.
Normal profit is the owner's opportunity cost and is included among implicit costs.

Production case 6: Riverbend Textiles has MP sequence 11, 14, 15, 13, 11, 9, 7, 5.

WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to wait until mp negative. Identify the first decline in MP and separate it from negative MP and long-run scale.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DIMINISHING MARGINAL PRODUCT

Horizontal axis: Workers; vertical axis: Total output. The TP line connects output 0 with no workers, about 8 with 1, 20 with 2, 34 with 3, 46 with 4, 56 with 5, 64 with 6, 70 with 7 and 74 with 8 workers. Output rises throughout; the line becomes flatter after the third worker. Values without printed point labels are approximate readings from the scale.

Total product rises from 34 units with three workers to 46 with four, so the fourth worker's marginal product is 12. The fifth worker raises output from 46 to 56, giving marginal product of 10. Output still increases, but the smaller addition shows diminishing marginal product.
